story.e:
**A question that comes to you at night.** The writer of Psalm 8 looks up at the sky. He sees the moon and the stars. And then he asks a question:

**What is a human being, that you remember him?** (8:5)

That is: there is all of that up there, and yet you **notice me**? How can that be?

The question is born out of feeling small. It is not a bad feeling — it is simply what a person feels when they are looking at something very large.

**The picture of the answer.** The psalm does not reply *because you are magnificent*. It says something else:

*You made him a little lower than God, and crowned him with glory and honour* (8:6).

So the dignity is **received**, not earned. It is not there because the human deserved it, but because someone placed it on him — like a crown.

Then the psalm lists what over: *you put everything under his feet* — the flocks, the wild beasts, the birds of the sky, the fish of the sea (8:7-9). That list is almost word for word the same as in **Genesis 1:26-28**, at the beginning of creation.

**And now look at the frame.** The psalm begins:

*Lord, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth!* (8:2)

And it **ends**:

*Lord, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth!* (8:10)

Exactly the same sentence. So the question *what is a human being* is not the **subject** of the psalm — it is its **middle**. The psalm is about God's name, and the question about humanity sits inside that frame.

**The same question, differently.** And now the most interesting thing in this part. In another place in the Bible almost exactly the same question is asked — but with an entirely different feeling. Job says this:

*What is a human being, that you make so much of him, and that you turn your attention to him? You visit him every morning, and you examine him every moment* (Job 7:17-18).

The same question — but Job is not marvelling. Job is **bitter**. What he wants is for God finally to **leave him alone**.

**So the same question in two ways.** For the psalmist, the wonder is that God looks. For Job, the trouble is that God looks. And in the Bible **both are there**.

**An honest sentence from the New Testament.** The letter to the Hebrews quotes this psalm, and then adds something very candid:

*You put everything under his feet. At present, however, we do not yet see everything subjected to him* (Hebrews 2:8).

That is: the writer of the letter says it himself — **the psalm's picture does not match what we see.** He does not pretend that it does. That is not weakness; it is honesty.
story.m:
**What is the psalm about?** This is worth settling first, because almost everyone sets it aside.

Verse **2** and verse **10** of Psalm 8 are word for word the same: *Lord, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth!* So the psalm is **framed by God's name**: its first and last sentence are identical.

It follows that the famous question *what is a human being* is **not the psalm's topic**. The psalm is about God, and the question about humanity stands in the middle of it, inside the frame.

This is not a small matter. If the psalm is quoted as though it were about human greatness, it has been cut out of its frame. The psalm says: *you are majestic* — and **within that** it marvels that such a one knows about him at all.

**The word in what is a human being.** In 8:5 the word for *human* is Hebrew **enosh**. This is not the word used for the great and strong. *Enosh* denotes the **mortal, frail, passing** human — the one who runs out.

So the question runs more precisely: *what is this fleeting little life, that it should mean something to you?*

And notice where the question comes from: from verse 4, where the psalmist **looks up at the sky**. Feeling small here is not a sin, not unbelief and not sorrow — it is what sets the question going. The psalm does not say do not feel small. It says you can speak from here too.

**An answer that is not flattery.** *You made him a little lower than God, and crowned him with glory and honour* (8:6).

Two things are in that:

**1. The place.** The human being is neither lowest nor highest. *A little lower* — exactly enough to be neither nothing nor God.

**2. The source of the dignity.** The verb *crowned* makes plain that **someone else gave it**. Not an inner property, not an achievement, not an earned rank. This is the same pattern we saw in Psalm 139: there it was *your eyes saw me when I was still unformed* — he was known before he had done anything.

**The list and Genesis 1.** 8:7-9 is almost word for word the list of **Genesis 1:26-28**: the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky, the animals of the earth. So the psalm tells the first chapter of the creation account **in verse**.

And one important order in Genesis 1:28: **the blessing comes before the task.** *God blessed them and said to them: be fruitful…* First a blessing, then work. It is not received for performance.

**And now the heart of this part: the same question, with the opposite feeling.**

Set the two side by side:

| | What does it ask? | With what feeling? |
|---|---|---|
| **Psalm 8:5** | what is a human being, that you remember him? | **wonder** — it is unbelievable that you notice |
| **Job 7:17** | what is a human being, that you make so much of him? | **bitterness** — why will you not leave me alone? |

Job's continuation is unmistakable: *you visit him every morning, and you examine him every moment* (7:18). For the psalmist God's attention is a **gift**. For Job it is a **burden**.

**What do we do with this?** Exactly what we did with Psalms 13 and 22 two parts ago, and with verses 7-12 of Psalm 139: **we say both, and we do not choose.**

Because both will be true at some point. There will be a day when it is good that someone knows about you. And there will be a day when it is too much that someone knows about you. **The Bible kept both sentences**, and corrected neither.

This part, incidentally, prepares something: soon in this module four parts deal with **the book of Job**. There this bitter voice will be the main character.

**The honesty of Hebrews 2.** The letter to the Hebrews quotes Psalm 8 (2:6), and then says:

*You put everything under his feet. At present, however, we do not yet see everything subjected to him* (2:8).

Read that again. The writer of the letter **quotes the Bible**, and then states that **this is not how it looks now**. He does not explain it away, does not smooth it over, and does not act as if he had failed to notice.

This is a very important example, because it shows that **the Bible also contains the places where the Bible itself admits the tension.** We need not cover it over either.
story.h:
**The frame as a rule of reading.** 8:2 and 8:10 are identical. This is the structural figure called **inclusio**: the text opens and closes with the same sentence, and in doing so marks what it is about.

The conclusion is firm, and worth stating: **Psalm 8 is not an anthropological text.** It is not a teaching about human dignity but praise of God's name, within which the question about humanity serves as an **example** of how majestic that name is.

So every citation that lifts 8:5-6 out of its frame and uses it as a statement about human greatness performs an operation the psalm does not perform.

**The translation question in 8:6.** This is one of the best-known translation divergences in the Psalms.

The Hebrew text: *vattechassereihu me'at **me'elohim***.

*Me'elohim* can mean:

- **than God** — the usual sense of the word (*Elohim* = God).
- **than the heavenly beings, than the angels** — the word *elohim* in the Hebrew Bible sometimes denotes heavenly beings or the divine court (for example Psalm 82:1).

The Greek **Septuagint** chose the *than the angels* reading, and from there **Hebrews 2:7** took it over, which likewise writes *angels*. Translations divide: some read *than God*, others *than the angels*.

**This question is not settled**, and cannot be settled from the text. Both are linguistically possible. If you read one in one Bible and the other in another, you have not found an error; you have found this question.

The difference is not trivial: *a little lower than God* is an unusually high claim about humanity; *a little lower than the angels* is more restrained.

**The text of 8:3.** *Through the mouths of little children and infants you also establish strength.* The Hebrew of this verse is hard: it is not clear exactly what the *strength* is, or how the silencing of the enemy connects to it. Translations differ here too.

One thing, though, is certain and interesting: **Jesus quotes this verse** in Matthew 21:16, when the children are shouting in the temple and the priests object. Jesus quotes the Septuagint text, where *praise* stands in place of *strength*.

**The plural let us make.** In Genesis 1:26 God speaks in the plural: *let us make human beings in our image.* There are several readings of this, and none is proven:

- a **royal or majestic plural** (the way a king speaks of himself),
- a **heavenly council** — God addressing his court (compare 1 Kings 22:19, Job 1:6),
- an **emphatic form** within Hebrew itself,
- in Christian tradition, a **trinitarian** reading.

Of these the last makes sense from the standpoint of Christian reading, but **it cannot be claimed that the Hebrew text originally said this**. The honest sentence: the plural is there; its explanation is open.

**The question of dominion — and what the Bible does not leave standing.** Genesis 1:26-28 used two Hebrew verbs: **radah** (to rule) and **kabash** (to subdue, to conquer). These are **strong words**. *Kabash* is the same verb used for taking possession of territory.

A great many things have been justified in history by appeal to these words — among them the idea that the world is a stock to be used up.

**But now read what stands two chapters later.** Genesis 2:15 says that God placed the human in the garden **to keep it and to tend it**. The two Hebrew verbs standing here are:

- **abad** — to serve, to work (the same verb is used for service and for worship),
- **shamar** — to keep, to guard, to watch over.

**So the same Bible, two chapters apart, gives two different verb pairs for the human task.** One speaks of dominion, the other of service and keeping.

Anyone who reads only the first gets a picture **the Bible itself does not leave standing**. And anyone who reads only the second leaves out that the task carries real responsibility and real power. Both stand there together.

**A third version of the same question.** The question *what is a human being* occurs three times in the Hebrew Bible, and all three sound different:

- **Psalm 8:5** — in wonder: *that you remember him?*
- **Job 7:17** — in bitterness: *that you make so much of him… examine him every moment?*
- **Psalm 144:3** — plainly, almost drily: *Lord, what is a human being, that you know of him?*

**Which came first, and who knew whose text, cannot be settled.** Most scholars hold that Job 7:17 is a **deliberate reversal** of Psalm 8 (or of the tradition behind it) — Job takes the words of praise and turns them into a complaint. This is likely and fits the procedure of the book of Job very well, but **it is not proven**: it is also possible that all three draw on an established form of the question.

**The tension in Hebrews 2:8.** The letter quotes the psalm, then writes: *at present, however, we do not yet see everything subjected to him.*

It is worth seeing what happens here. A New Testament writer:

1. quotes Scripture,
2. states that what the text says **is not visible in experience**,
3. **does not resolve** this with an explanation,
4. but moves the question instead: *but we do see that… God crowned Jesus with glory* (2:9).

This is not smoothing over: the *not yet* stays where it is. And notice what 2:9 runs out to: it ties the crown not to the taking of power but to **the suffering of death**. Here too the source of dignity is not strength.

**What the text does NOT say.** Six things:

**1. It does not say the human earned his dignity.** The verb *crowned* means precisely the opposite.

**2. It does not settle whether it is lower than God or lower than the angels.** That is a translation question, and it is open.

**3. It does not say what exactly the dominion is for.** What it means in practice the psalm does not unfold — and Genesis 2:15 adds a different emphasis to it.

**4. It does not say the world may be used up.** This is the most important negative here, because it is what people tend to read out of it. *Put under his feet* means responsibility, not free use — and the Bible itself sets another verb pair beside it.

**5. It does not say when the not yet of Hebrews 2:8 comes to an end.** The letter uses the words *not yet*, and gives no date.

**6. It does not resolve the difference between Psalm 8 and Job 7.** Both are there, side by side, permanently.

**One last note.** This part works from four places: a psalm, a creation account, a lament and a New Testament letter. All four hold **the same question** in their hands, and none of them closes it.

That is not a fault of the Bible. That is the nature of the question.

verse.text: what is a human being, that you remember him, and a son of man, that you care for him?

bio.hu: Dávid őt állította az éneklők élére, és tizenkét zsoltár viseli a nevét. Nem szép szavakat írt: az egyik zsoltárában bevallja, hogy majdnem megcsúszott a lába, mert látta, milyen jól megy a gőgösöknek. Nem titkolta el ezt a haragot — leírta, és úgy vitte Isten elé. Az ő énekes utódai még hetven évvel később, a hazatérés után is ott álltak és énekeltek.
bio.en: David put him in charge of the singers, and twelve psalms bear his name. He did not write pretty words: in one of his psalms he admits that his feet almost slipped, because he saw how well things went for the proud. He did not hide that anger — he wrote it down and brought it to God that way. His singer descendants were still standing and singing seventy years later, after the return home.

en.q: What did David put Asaph in charge of?
How many psalms bear Asaph's name?

hu.q: Mit vallott be az egyik zsoltárában?

en.q: What did he admit in one of his psalms?
What troubled Asaph?
o: That things went well for the proud
That he had too few singers
That he was not invited to the palace

en.q: What did he do with that anger?
o: He wrote it down and brought it to God

hu.q: Hol fordult meg a zsoltár hangulata?

en.q: Where did the mood of the psalm turn?
o: When he went into God's sanctuary
When he received a new song

hu.q: Kik énekeltek a hazatérés után is?

en.q: Who was still singing after the return home?

hu.q: Igaz vagy hamis: Istenhez csak szép és megnyugtató szavakkal lehet szólni.

en.q: True or false: we may speak to God only with pretty, calming words.
What does Asaph teach about complaint?
o: A complaint can also be prayer
Only a cheerful person may pray

bio.hu: Három fiú, akiket Dániellel együtt hurcoltak el, és még a nevüket is elvették tőlük. Amikor a király hatalmas arany szobrot állított, és a zenére mindenkinek le kellett borulnia, ők állva maradtak. A mondatuk a történet lelke: van Istenünk, aki meg tud szabadítani — de ha nem szabadít meg, akkor sem szolgáljuk a te isteneidet. Megkötözve estek a tűzbe, és a király négy embert látott benne járkálni.
bio.en: Three boys carried off together with Daniel, who even had their names taken from them. When the king set up a huge golden statue and everyone had to bow down at the music, they stayed standing. Their sentence is the heart of the story: we have a God who can rescue us — but if he does not rescue us, we still will not serve your gods. They fell into the fire tied up, and the king saw four men walking about in it.

hu.q: Mit vettek el a három fiútól a fogságban?

en.q: What was taken from the three boys in exile?
What did the king set up?
At what did everyone have to bow down?
o: At a horn blast in the morning
Ha nem szabadít meg Isten, akkor sem szolgálunk másnak

en.q: What did they answer the king?
o: Even if God does not rescue us, we will not serve another
We did not hear the music

hu.q: Mit tett a király a kemencével?

en.q: What did the king do to the furnace?
o: He had it heated seven times hotter

hu.q: Hány embert látott a király a tűzben?

en.q: How many men did the king see in the fire?

hu.q: Mi történt a hajukkal és a ruhájukkal?

en.q: What happened to their hair and clothes?
o: Nothing, they did not even smell of smoke

hu.q: Igaz vagy hamis: azért maradtak hűségesek, mert biztosak voltak a szabadulásban.

en.q: True or false: they stayed faithful because they were sure of being rescued.

o: A hűség nem a jó végtől függ
Csak akkor érdemes hűségesnek lenni, ha megmenekülünk

en.q: What do the three boys teach?
o: Faithfulness does not depend on a happy ending
It is worth being faithful only if we are saved

bio.hu: Zsidó ember Súsán várában, aki a szülők nélkül maradt Esztert felnevelte. Egyszer leleplezett egy összeesküvést a király ellen, és feljegyezték a könyvbe — de évekig semmit nem kapott érte. Hámán előtt nem hajolt meg, és ezért az egész népét veszélybe hozta. Nem hallgatott: gyászruhát vett, és ő üzente Eszternek a kérdést, ami az egész könyv fordulópontja.
bio.en: A Jewish man in the fortress of Susa who raised Esther when she was left without parents. Once he uncovered a plot against the king, and it was written in the book — but for years he received nothing for it. He would not bow before Haman, and so brought his whole people into danger. He did not keep silent: he put on mourning clothes, and it was he who sent Esther the question that turns the whole book.

en.q: In which city did Mordecai live?
Whom did he raise?
What did he uncover?
What happened with his reward?
Before whom would he not bow?

hu.q: Mit tett, amikor meghallotta a nép elleni rendeletet?
o: Gyászruhát vett és hamut szórt magára

en.q: What did he do when he heard the decree against his people?
o: He put on mourning clothes and ashes
He went to the palace shouting
Ki tudja, nem ezért az időért jutottál-e oda?

en.q: What message did he send Esther?
o: Who knows whether you came to this place for such a time?

hu.q: Mi lett Mordokajból a könyv végén?

en.q: What did Mordecai become at the end of the book?
o: Second in rank after the king
Ki kell mondani, amit látunk, akkor is, ha veszélyes
Mindig meg kell hajolni a hatalom előtt

en.q: What does Mordecai's story teach?
o: We must say what we see, even when it is dangerous
It is better not to speak

bio.hu: Héber neve Hadassza volt. Nem ő döntött úgy, hogy a palotába megy: elvitték. Évekig titkolta, hogy zsidó. Amikor az egész népe veszélybe került, három napos böjtöt kért, és hívatlanul bement a királyhoz, pedig ezért halál járt. Ennyit mondott: ha elveszek, elveszek. Isten neve a könyvben egyetlenegyszer sem szerepel — mégis minden megfordul.
bio.en: Her Hebrew name was Hadassah. It was not her choice to go to the palace: she was taken. For years she kept hidden that she was Jewish. When her whole people came into danger she asked for a three-day fast and went in to the king uninvited, though that carried the death penalty. She said only this: if I perish, I perish. God's name never appears once in the book — yet everything turns around.

en.q: What was Esther's Hebrew name?
How did she come to the palace?
o: She was taken, it was not her choice
She was invited as a guest

en.q: What did she keep hidden for years?

hu.q: Mit kért, mielőtt a királyhoz ment?

en.q: What did she ask for before going to the king?

hu.q: Miért volt veszélyes bemenni a királyhoz?

en.q: Why was it dangerous to go in to the king?
o: Going uninvited carried the death penalty
The throne room was far away

en.q: What did Esther say before she set out?
How many banquets did she hold before she spoke?

o: Isten neve egyszer sem szerepel benne

en.q: What is unusual about the book of Esther?
o: God's name never appears in it
There is no king in it

hu.q: Mit tanít Eszter története a bátorságról?
o: Félni és mégis odamenni: ez a bátorság

en.q: What does Esther's story teach about courage?
o: To be afraid and go anyway: that is courage
A brave person feels no fear

bio.hu: A perzsa király pohárnoka volt — jó állás, biztonságos élet. Amikor meghallotta, hogy Jeruzsálem falai romokban állnak, leült és napokig sírt, böjtölt, imádkozott. Aztán megrémült a király előtt, de mégis kért: engedélyt, fát, leveleket. Éjjel egyedül körüljárta a romokat, és ötvenkét nap alatt felépült a fal. Egyik kezükben a szerszám, a másikban a fegyver.
bio.en: He was cupbearer to the Persian king — a good post and a safe life. When he heard that the walls of Jerusalem lay in ruins he sat down and wept for days, fasting and praying. Then he was terrified before the king, yet he asked anyway: for permission, for timber, for letters. At night he rode around the ruins alone, and in fifty-two days the wall was finished. A tool in one hand, a weapon in the other.

hu.q: Mi volt Nehémia munkája a perzsa királynál?

en.q: What was Nehemiah's work for the Persian king?
What news did he receive about Jerusalem?
o: That its walls lay in ruins
That there was a new king

en.q: What did he do first when he heard?

hu.q: Hogyan érezte magát, amikor a király előtt szólt?

en.q: How did he feel when he spoke before the king?
o: He was terrified, but asked anyway

hu.q: Mit tett az első éjjel Jeruzsálemben?

en.q: What did he do on his first night in Jerusalem?
o: He went around the ruins alone

hu.q: Hány nap alatt épült fel a fal?

en.q: In how many days was the wall finished?

hu.q: Mi volt az építők két kezében?

en.q: What was in the builders' two hands?

hu.q: Mit felelt, amikor a gúnyolódók tárgyalásra hívták?
o: Nagy munkát végzek, nem mehetek le

en.q: What did he answer when the mockers called him to a meeting?
o: I am doing a great work, I cannot come down
Az imádság és a kemény munka együtt jár

en.q: What does Nehemiah's story teach?
o: Prayer and hard work go together

bio.hu: Pap és írástudó, aki egy egész csoportot vezetett haza Babilonból. Nem kért katonai kíséretet az útra, inkább böjtöt rendelt. Róla azt írja a Biblia, hogy szívből törekedett arra, hogy kutassa, megtegye és tanítsa Isten törvényét — ebben a sorrendben. A nagy téren hajnaltól délig olvasta fel a könyvet, és a léviták elmagyarázták, hogy a nép értse is, amit hall.
bio.en: A priest and scribe who led a whole group home from Babylon. He did not ask for a military escort for the journey; he called a fast instead. The Bible says of him that he set his heart to study, to do and to teach God's law — in that order. In the great square he read the book aloud from dawn until noon, and the Levites explained it so that the people would also understand what they heard.

en.q: What was Ezra?
From where did he lead the group home?
What did he not ask for on the journey?
What did he call instead?

hu.q: Mi volt a három dolog, amire a szívét szánta?
o: Kutatni, megtenni és tanítani a törvényt

en.q: What were the three things he set his heart on?
o: To study, to do and to teach the law

hu.q: Meddig olvasta fel a könyvet a téren?

en.q: How long did he read the book aloud in the square?

o: Hogy elmagyarázzák, amit a nép hall

en.q: Why were the Levites there?
o: To explain what the people heard

hu.q: Mit tett a nép, amikor meghallotta a törvényt?

en.q: What did the people do when they heard the law?

hu.q: Mit mondtak nekik a sírás helyett?
o: Az Úrban való öröm a ti erősségetek

en.q: What were they told instead of weeping?
o: The joy of the Lord is your strength
Nem elég felolvasni, érteni is kell

en.q: What does Ezra's story teach?
o: Reading aloud is not enough, it must be understood
The book belongs only to the priests
